item.title: Is It Normal for a Grieving Person to Feel Happiness?
item.description:
Grief

Is It Normal for a Grieving Person to Feel Happiness?

Personal Perspective: Sadness was expected, but happiness showed up, too.

Posted August 25, 2026

Source: Tookapic/Pixabay

“The husband I treasured had disappeared. Why was I happy?” That was the subtitle of a recent article in the New York Times by writer Annie Korzen, describing her feelings after her husband's death. Like me and my longtime romantic partner Brian, who died this year, she and her husband were in their 80s. They had an even longer relationship than ours—60 years!—as compared with our mere 30 years together. Also like me, she coped with an intense period of caregiving before the death.

One might expect there would be some relief mingled with Korzen’s sorrow. But happiness? Yes. She writes, “I have rediscovered the simple joys of everyday life and, to my great astonishment, I have frequent flashes of something I thought I would never feel again: I believe it’s called happiness. Please don’t judge me.”

Too many people would judge Korzen’s experience. We have an image of what grief is supposed to look like—tears, sackcloth and ashes, depression, widow’s weeds. Korzen is brave for contravening the accepted stereotypes of mourning and being honest about her experience. In the “Comments” section about her article, the avalanche of positive remarks about Korzen’s essay attests to the fact that her experience might be more common than we know.

My Experience of Grief: Happiness, Sadness…and More

Like Korzen, I have experienced many moments of happiness since my partner's death. Now that I am newly single, I have the freedom to spend my time as I please. If I want to watch junk TV, I watch junk TV. If I want to read, I read. If I want to “import” prepared food from my favorite supermarket instead of cooking from scratch, I do it.

But my happiness is mingled with a host of other emotions, ones that often descend on me unexpectedly. These emotions include grief, nostalgia, anger, fear, vulnerability, and many more. I’ve also experienced the emotions in the Stages-of-Grief model—denial, anger, depression, acceptance—not necessarily in sequence, but randomly.

To illustrate: One Sunday I decided to go out for lunch by myself. I chose a new restaurant that was just the kind of place that Brian and I would have enjoyed together.

And it was a lovely place. The coffee was robust, the food was delicious, and the service friendly. The panini was scrumptious. The side of crispy potatoes was unusually tasty, too. Moreover, I was proud that I had taken a few courageous steps to eat out alone.

Suddenly my joy turned to sadness as I realized I couldn’t share this moment with Brian. He and I always relished the experience of a new restaurant. Specifically, I yearned to tell Brian how delicious the potatoes were. Brian loved potatoes—part of his Irish heritage, he would say—and he would have savored these. Tears filled my eyes.

Source: Pastel100/Pixabay

But then the server whisked my plate away and came back with a tiramisu. My tears and my sadness melted away as I savored the amazing flavors of the tiramisu.

Am I shallow? I asked myself. Could my grief be so easily tamed by a sweet treat? Was there something wrong with me?

Often since Brian’s death, I had spotted a photo of the two of us and felt overwhelming nostalgia for the times we had spent together. Or I would remember something sweet he had said to me. During these times, I would find myself teary and choked up. But crying over fried potatoes? Who gets hijacked by hash browns?

The Dual Process Model of Grief

By chance, I discovered a psychological model that explained my strange experiences of grief. The model, termed “The Dual Process Model of Grief," from a paper by social psychologists Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, is beautifully summarized here at the website of The Loss Foundation.

“The Dual Process Model of Grief...suggests that it’s natural to move back and forth between focusing on your loss and focusing on daily life. Grieving isn’t a straight line—it’s a process of oscillation between confronting and avoiding the pain of loss.”

I’m not sure “avoiding” is the right word here—maybe “rebounding from” or even “reengaging with daily life” might be more apt. Of prime importance, however, this model does affirm that it is normal for someone who is grieving to have both loss-oriented feelings—remembering the deceased, mourning the loss—and restoration-oriented feelings—the desire to create new routines, make new friends, and get on with life.

The Loss Foundation website further states: “The Dual Process Model explains why we naturally move in and out of grief. It shows that spending time with your grief (feeling, remembering, mourning) and taking time away from it (functioning, distracting, even enjoying [my italics]) are both important for coping and healing.”

Even enjoying. For many people in the throes of the grief process, “enjoying life” may feel too much like a betrayal of the beloved person. This model gives permission to enjoy life without guilt. "Enjoying" is viewed as an aspect of healing.

The dual-process “oscillation model” describes my emotional experiences to a T—the ebbs and flows of both grief and joy—and normalizes them. It is reassuring to know that I am not the only one who has both laughed and cried at odd times and places after the loss of a loved one. In her blog about the stress of both grieving and recovering, PT blogger Sophia Dembling writes, “I have cried in Costco more than once.” Yes, I get it.

Take-Home Tips

If you are in mourning, try these tips from the Dual Process Model, suggested on The Loss Foundation website:

  1. Allow yourself to feel grief when it shows up, and to step back when you need a breather.
  2. Notice what helps you engage with grief, and what helps you recover from it.
  3. Reflect on what “loss-oriented” and “restoration-oriented” days look like for you; both are important for healing.

I would add two more tips:

  1. Keep your self-care program in place—exercise, eat well, get plenty of sleep, connect with others.
  2. Most of all, accept all your emotions—your grief and also your happiness...and all the messy feelings that accompany them.

Summing Up

The Dual Process Model reinforces the idea that there is no one “right” way to grieve, and that feelings of happiness can be a normal part of grief recovery. I consider this model especially powerful and beautiful because it neither denies death nor denies life.

Looking back on my recent experiences, I now find it completely natural that I cried over the hash browns and felt joy as I tasted the tiramisu. You can feel grief and enjoy your dessert, too.
